Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 73
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Forester
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 79

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women, Auditory (Sounds): Related sounds, Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Exercise: Exercise, Compulsive Spending: I spend money impulsively to distract or comfort myself, Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person

Vignette:
Ingrid Schmidt was seventy-three years old, a forester by trade, and she had spent the last fifty years walking the same pine stands and logging roads in northern Minnesota. She knew the land well—knew which trails would flood in spring, where the oaks grew thickest, how to read a change in the wind. But she did not trust people, and she especially did not trust women. When a female coworker at the ranger station asked to speak with her privately, Ingrid would find an excuse to keep the door open or to meet in the hallway instead. If a woman came to her cabin to deliver a package or to check on her, Ingrid would stand on the porch rather than invite her inside. Being alone with a woman, even one she had known for years, made her feel small and watchful—like a child again, waiting for the mood to shift. Her mother had been a woman, and her mother had hurt her. That lesson had never faded: the person who is supposed to care for you can be the one who harms you, and you can never know if the same is true of anyone else.

The quiet had been like that in the house where she grew up. Her mother—a woman who could go from calm to cold in the space of a breath—would stop speaking, and Ingrid would know. In the silence, before the blows came, there was only the sound of her mother’s breathing, and then the flat crack of a hand against her face, against her back, against the backs of her legs. She had learned to read those silences better than she could read any map. She had learned that trust was a trap. That belief had never left her. It had settled into her bones. As an adult, she did what she could to keep the world from surprising her. She worked in the forest because it was open, and she could see what was coming. But she avoided being alone in rooms or buildings—especially if a woman was in them. At the ranger station, she kept her office door propped open and never closed it when a female colleague came in. She stayed in the common areas where others were present. At home, a small cabin she had bought after her divorce, she left the television on constantly. The hum of voices filled the space and kept the quiet at bay—and it also meant that if a woman visited, there was always sound to break the closeness.

But the forest itself was inescapable, and the sounds were everywhere. The snap of a twig underfoot, the rustle of leaves—these sounds were ordinary, but sometimes they were not. Sometimes a sound would match a sound from long ago, and her whole body would lock. On those days, she would find a reason to head back to the truck, to sit behind the wheel with the engine running and the radio on, just to hear something steady and human. She also avoided anything she thought of as deliberate exercise. The physical demands of her job—long hikes, hauling equipment, clearing brush—had become harder, but she would drive her truck as close as possible to a worksite rather than walk the extra mile. Moving her body in a certain way reminded her of the forced physical exertion her mother had demanded—the scrubbing, the lifting, the standing until her legs ached. So she kept still when she could.

She had come to believe that her life had been destroyed by those years, that whatever person she might have become had been taken from her. She often said she felt like an object, not a person. She meant it literally. She did not feel that she existed in the same way other people did. Money had become a strange comfort. She spent impulsively—tools she did not need, clothing she never wore, subscriptions to things she never used. The act of buying gave her a few minutes of distraction. But the consequences had caught up with her. Her savings were nearly gone, and she had taken to borrowing against her retirement. Her daughter, who lived in another state, had called after noticing the credit card bills. Ingrid had not told her about the spending, or the triggers, or the years of believing that she was not quite real. She had simply said she was fine.

It was the silence that finally brought her in—and the women. She had been alone in the cabin one evening, the television on, when a loud noise from outside startled her. She muted the TV to listen, and the sudden absence of sound was worse than the noise. She stood frozen, her heart hammering. But what made her call the clinic the next morning was a moment from earlier that week: a female neighbor had stopped by unexpectedly, and Ingrid had pretended not to be home, crouching behind the couch until the woman left. She had felt like a child hiding from her mother. She was afraid of what would happen if she kept going this way—afraid that the silence would catch up with her, afraid that she would never be able to be in a room with a woman again without trembling. She hoped, though she could barely admit it, that someone might see her and help her become something more than an object that had learned to survive.
